items.stem: State what is meant by the term "air resistance".
items.answer: Friction caused by air acting against an object moving through it
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: friction caused by air acting against an object moving through it. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between friction and air resistance.
items.answer: Friction acts between solid surfaces sliding or gripping; air resistance is a type of friction from air on an object moving through it.
items.markingKey: Friction acts between solid surfaces sliding or gripping; air resistance is a type of friction from air on an object moving through it. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why friction can be useful and also a problem.
items.answer: Useful: it allows walking, gripping and braking; a problem: it wears parts and wastes energy as heat in machines.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Useful: it allows walking, gripping and braking; a problem: it wears parts and wastes energy as heat in machines. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Jonas plans to investigate how the type of surface affects the friction force on a sliding block. State three variables that must be controlled to make this a fair test.
items.answer: Any three of: mass of the block; the same block and side; pulling horizontally at a steady speed; the same newton meter
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 3: mass of the block – heavier blocks have more friction; the same block and side – surface of the block affects friction; pulling horizontally at a steady speed – angle and acceleration change the reading; the same newton meter – meters differ. The independent or dependent variable scores 0.

items.stem:
Isabel added masses on top of a block and measured the force needed to pull it at a steady speed across a bench.

Total mass / g | Friction force / N: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
200 | 0.73 | 0.71 | 0.69
400 | 1.40 | 1.41 | 1.40
600 | 2.10 | 2.23 | 2.11
800 | 2.83 | 2.94 | 2.82
1000 | 3.52 | 3.48 | 3.52

Calculate the percentage change in the mean friction force between 200 g and 1000 g.
items.markingKey: M1 means 0.71 and 3.51; M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100; A1 +393.9% (increase).

items.stem: A skydiver jumps from a plane. Draw (describe) force diagrams for the moment she leaves the plane, when falling at constant speed, and just after the parachute opens, and explain her motion at each stage.
items.answer: Leaving: weight large downwards, tiny air resistance – accelerates. Constant (terminal) speed: weight = air resistance (balanced arrows) – constant speed. Parachute opens: air resistance much larger than weight – decelerates until a new, lower terminal speed when forces balance again.
items.markingKey: Leaving: weight large downwards, tiny air resistance – accelerates. Constant (terminal) speed: weight = air resistance (balanced arrows) – constant speed. Parachute opens: air resistance much larger than weight – decelerates until a new, lower terminal speed when forces balance again.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Friction caused by air acting against an object moving through it"?
items.answer: air resistance
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of air resistance.

items.stem: "A moving object must have a force pushing it forward." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: An object can keep moving at constant speed with no resultant force; forces are needed only to change speed or direction.
items.markingKey: An object can keep moving at constant speed with no resultant force; forces are needed only to change speed or direction. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A newton meter reads 4.0 N when a wooden block is pulled at a steady speed across a desk. When sandpaper is placed under the block, it reads 5.0 N. By how much did the friction force increase, and why?
items.answer: 1.0 N; the rougher surface increases friction
items.markingKey: M1 5.0 − 4.0; A1 1.0 N; B1 at steady speed pull = friction; rougher surface → more friction.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The SI unit of speed (metres per second)"?
items.answer: m/s
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of m/s.

items.stem: Distinguish between the speed of a car and its velocity.
items.answer: Speed is how fast something moves (distance per time); velocity is speed in a given direction.
items.markingKey: Speed is how fast something moves (distance per time); velocity is speed in a given direction. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how to use a distance–time graph to find speed.
items.answer: Choose two points on a straight section; speed = change in distance ÷ change in time (the gradient).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Choose two points on a straight section; speed = change in distance ÷ change in time (the gradient). (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "A line going down on a distance–time graph means the object is slowing down." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: It means the object is moving back towards the start; slowing down is shown by a curve that becomes less steep.
items.markingKey: It means the object is moving back towards the start; slowing down is shown by a curve that becomes less steep. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the height of a ramp affects the average speed of a toy car travelling down it, state the dependent variable and describe how Rafael should measure it.
items.answer: average speed = 1.0 m ÷ time measured with light gates
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: average speed = 1.0 m ÷ time measured with light gates.

items.stem:
Jonas recorded the distance travelled by a cyclist every 10 s using a GPS app (three rides on the same route).

Time / s | Distance / m: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
10 | 53 | 52 | 51
20 | 101 | 102 | 106
30 | 158 | 154 | 150
40 | 213 | 203 | 208
50 | 251 | 260 | 267

State the time at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 50 s; range = 16 m; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 50 s; 1 range = max − min = 267 − 251 = 16 m; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: Elena investigated how the height of a ramp affects the average speed of a toy car travelling down it. The method had this weakness: the car hit the side of the ramp on some runs. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: add guide rails and discard runs where the car hits the sides
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: add guide rails and discard runs where the car hits the sides

items.stem: "Average speed cameras should replace all fixed speed cameras." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: They are more effective on long stretches of road, but cost and privacy must be balanced.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: stop drivers braking just at cameras; smoother traffic and fewer crashes. Arguments against: more expensive to install; privacy concerns about tracking cars. Supported judgement: They are more effective on long stretches of road, but cost and privacy must be balanced. Markbands (8 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Briefly explain why the speed shown on a car speedometer is different from the average speed for a journey.
items.answer: The speedometer shows the instantaneous speed, which changes; the average speed is total distance ÷ total time, including stops.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The speedometer shows the instantaneous speed, which changes; the average speed is total distance ÷ total time, including stops. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between average speed and instantaneous speed.
items.answer: Average speed is total distance ÷ total time for a journey; instantaneous speed is the speed at one moment.
items.markingKey: Average speed is total distance ÷ total time for a journey; instantaneous speed is the speed at one moment. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline one way in which Average speed cameras shows speed = distance ÷ time in technology.
items.answer: Pairs of cameras record a car’s number plate at two points a known distance apart; the time between gives average speed, catching drivers who slow only near single cameras. They have reduced speeding and crashes on many roads.
items.markingKey: Context (Pairs of cameras record a car’s number plate at two points a known distance apart; the time between gives average speed, catching drivers who slow only near single cameras.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: They have reduced speeding and crashes on many roads. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to speed = distance ÷ time in technology.

items.stem: A cyclist rides 6 km in 20 min, stops for 10 min, then rides 9 km in 30 min. Describe the distance–time graph and calculate the speed for each section and the average speed in km/h.
items.answer: Section 1: straight line rising 6 km in 20 min → 18 km/h. Stop: horizontal line for 10 min (0 km/h). Section 2: straight line rising 9 km in 30 min → 18 km/h (same gradient). Average = 15 km ÷ 1 h = 15 km/h.
items.markingKey: Section 1: straight line rising 6 km in 20 min → 18 km/h. Stop: horizontal line for 10 min (0 km/h). Section 2: straight line rising 9 km in 30 min → 18 km/h (same gradient). Average = 15 km ÷ 1 h = 15 km/h.

items.stem: What happens to a stationary object if the forces on it are balanced?
items.answer: It stays still
items.markingKey: It stays still. Newton’s first law.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a ball thrown upwards slows down.
items.answer: Weight (and air resistance) act downwards, opposite to its motion, giving a resultant force that decelerates it.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Weight (and air resistance) act downwards, opposite to its motion, giving a resultant force that decelerates it. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "A stationary object has no forces acting on it." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Forces act on it (e.g. weight and reaction force) but they are balanced.
items.markingKey: Forces act on it (e.g. weight and reaction force) but they are balanced. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Mateo used a data logger to record the speed of a falling cupcake case at different times after release.

Time / s | Speed / m/s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.1 | 0.52 | 0.52 | 0.51
0.2 | 0.76 | 0.76 | 0.78
0.4 | 0.98 | 1.00 | 0.95
0.6 | 1.01 | 1.02 | 1.05
0.8 | 1.06 | 0.99 | 1.05

State the time at which the repeat readings are least consistent, and calculate the range of the readings at that value. Suggest one way to make the data more reliable.
items.answer: 0.8 s; range = 0.07 m/s; e.g. take more repeats and discard anomalies / use more precise apparatus
items.markingKey: 1 0.8 s; 1 range = max − min = 1.06 − 0.99 = 0.07 m/s; 1 valid improvement (more repeats, more precise instrument, control a named variable).

items.stem: Jonas wants to find out how the area of a paper parachute affects its terminal velocity. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does area of the parachute canopy affect time to fall the last 1.0 m of a 2.5 m drop?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (area of the parachute canopy (100, 200, 300, 400, 500 cm²)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (time to fall the last 1.0 m of a 2.5 m drop (used to calculate terminal velocity)) in a question form.

items.stem: Yusuf pulls a trolley forwards with a force of 50 N. Friction acts backwards with a force of 10 N. Calculate the resultant force and describe the effect on the motion of a trolley.
items.answer: 40 N forwards; it speeds up
items.markingKey: M1 resultant = 50 − 10; A1 40 N forwards; B1 effect on motion.

items.stem: Chloé plans an investigation into how the area of a paper parachute affects its terminal velocity. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (area of the parachute canopy (100, 200, 300, 400, 500 cm²)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: A rocket of weight 20 000 N has an engine thrust of 26 000 N at launch. Calculate the resultant force and describe and explain how the rocket’s motion and the forces change as it rises and burns fuel.
items.answer: Resultant = 26 000 − 20 000 = 6000 N upwards – rocket accelerates upwards. As fuel burns, mass and weight decrease so resultant force increases (if thrust constant) – acceleration increases; air resistance increases with speed, reducing the resultant; higher up, air is thinner and gravity slightly weaker.
items.markingKey: Resultant = 26 000 − 20 000 = 6000 N upwards – rocket accelerates upwards. As fuel burns, mass and weight decrease so resultant force increases (if thrust constant) – acceleration increases; air resistance increases with speed, reducing the resultant; higher up, air is thinner and gravity slightly weaker.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a skydiver reaches a terminal velocity.
items.answer: As speed increases, air resistance increases until it equals weight; the resultant force is zero so the speed stays constant.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: As speed increases, air resistance increases until it equals weight; the resultant force is zero so the speed stays constant. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between unbalanced forces and balanced forces.
items.answer: Balanced forces give zero resultant force, so an object stays still or moves at constant velocity; unbalanced forces give a resultant that changes speed or direction.
items.markingKey: Balanced forces give zero resultant force, so an object stays still or moves at constant velocity; unbalanced forces give a resultant that changes speed or direction. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Using Isaac Newton’s laws of motion (1687) as an example, explain laws of motion.
items.answer: In the Principia, Newton stated that an object stays at rest or constant velocity unless a resultant force acts, and that force causes acceleration. His laws explained motion on Earth and of the planets and are still used to design vehicles and launch spacecraft.
items.markingKey: Context (In the Principia, Newton stated that an object stays at rest or constant velocity unless a resultant force acts, and that force causes acceleration.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: His laws explained motion on Earth and of the planets and are still used to design vehicles and launch spacecraft. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to laws of motion.

items.stem: What happens to your mass if you travel to the Moon?
items.answer: It stays the same
items.markingKey: A. Weight changes, mass does not.

items.stem: Briefly explain why an object’s weight is different on different planets.
items.answer: Weight = mass × gravitational field strength, and g depends on the mass and size of the planet.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Weight = mass × gravitational field strength, and g depends on the mass and size of the planet. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "There is no gravity in space." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Gravity acts throughout space; astronauts in orbit feel weightless because they are in free fall around the Earth.
items.markingKey: Gravity acts throughout space; astronauts in orbit feel weightless because they are in free fall around the Earth. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A 12 kg probe has a weight of 19.2 N on the Moon. Calculate the gravitational field strength there.
items.answer: 1.6 N/kg

items.stem:
Isabel measured the weight of different masses with a newton meter, three times each.

Mass / kg | Weight / N: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.1 | 0.92 | 0.90 | 0.88
0.2 | 1.73 | 1.84 | 1.73
0.3 | 2.68 | 2.59 | 2.62
0.4 | 3.64 | 3.64 | 3.48
0.5 | 4.49 | 4.54 | 4.58

Calculate the mean weight when the mass was 0.4 kg.
items.markingKey: M1 (3.64 + 3.64 + 3.48) ÷ 3; A1 3.59 N (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Space tourism should be encouraged."
items.answer: Space tourism brings some benefits, but environmental and fairness concerns mean it should be regulated.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: inspires interest in science; funds development of new technology. Arguments against: huge fuel use and emissions per passenger; only for the very wealthy; safety risks. Supported judgement: Space tourism brings some benefits, but environmental and fairness concerns mean it should be regulated.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The force of gravity on an object, measured in newtons (N)"?
items.answer: weight
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of weight.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Apollo 15 hammer and feather (1971) shows gravity and air resistance.
items.answer: Astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon; with no air resistance, they hit the ground together. It confirmed Galileo’s idea that all objects fall with the same acceleration without air resistance.
items.markingKey: Context (Astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon; with no air resistance, they hit the ground together.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It confirmed Galileo’s idea that all objects fall with the same acceleration without air resistance. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to gravity and air resistance.

items.stem: Rafael plans an investigation into how the mass of an object affects its weight. Describe how the results should be recorded, processed and presented, and explain how the reliability and validity of the conclusion will be judged.
items.answer: Results table with the independent variable (mass hung on a newton meter (100, 200, 300, 400, 500 g)) in the first column and repeat readings of the dependent variable with units in headings; calculate means (ignoring anomalies); plot a suitable graph of the mean dependent variable against the independent variable with a line of best fit; describe the trend and compare with the hypothesis; judge reliability from the spread of repeats and validity from how well variables were controlled.
items.markingKey: 1 table with IV, repeats and units; 1 means calculated, anomalies identified and excluded; 1 appropriate graph (line graph/scatter for continuous IV, bar chart for categorical) with line of best fit; 1 trend compared with hypothesis; 1 reliability (spread of repeats) and validity (controls) discussed.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "principle of moments".
items.answer: For a balanced object, total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: for a balanced object, total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why camels have large flat feet.
items.answer: They spread the camel’s weight over a large area, reducing pressure so they do not sink into sand.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They spread the camel’s weight over a large area, reducing pressure so they do not sink into sand. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "The moment only depends on how hard you push." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The moment also depends on the perpendicular distance from the pivot.
items.markingKey: The moment also depends on the perpendicular distance from the pivot. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Rafael balanced a metre rule on a pivot at its centre, hung a 2 N weight 20 cm to the left and found the force needed at different distances to the right (three trials each).

Distance on the right / cm | Force needed to balance / N: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
10 | 4.12 | 4.09 | 4.36
20 | 2.13 | 2.13 | 2.03
25 | 1.70 | 1.69 | 1.75
40 | 1.07 | 1.07 | 1.03
50 | 0.87 | 0.82 | 0.83

Calculate the mean force needed to balance when the distance on the right was 25 cm.
items.markingKey: M1 (1.70 + 1.69 + 1.75) ÷ 3; A1 1.71 N (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: Leila wants to find out how the depth of water affects the pressure at a point. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does depth below the water surface affect distance a jet of water squirts horizontally from holes at each depth in a tall bottle?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (depth below the water surface (5, 10, 15, 20, 25 cm)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (distance a jet of water squirts horizontally from holes at each depth in a tall bottle) in a question form.

items.stem: A 40 kg child sits 1.5 m from the pivot of a seesaw. Where must a 60 kg adult sit to balance it? Explain your working using the principle of moments, and explain why the seesaw tips if the adult moves further away. (g = 10 N/kg)
items.answer: Child weight 400 N, moment = 400 × 1.5 = 600 N m anticlockwise. Adult weight 600 N; balance: 600 × d = 600 → d = 1.0 m. Moving further increases the adult’s moment above 600 N m, so clockwise > anticlockwise and the seesaw tips towards the adult.
items.markingKey: Child weight 400 N, moment = 400 × 1.5 = 600 N m anticlockwise. Adult weight 600 N; balance: 600 × d = 600 → d = 1.0 m. Moving further increases the adult’s moment above 600 N m, so clockwise > anticlockwise and the seesaw tips towards the adult.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "For a balanced object, total clockwise moment = total anticlockwise moment"?
items.answer: principle of moments
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of principle of moments.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Archimedes and levers shows principle of moments.
items.answer: Archimedes explained the law of the lever and is quoted as saying “Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth.” Levers are used in wheelbarrows, crowbars, scissors and the human arm.
items.markingKey: Context (Archimedes explained the law of the lever and is quoted as saying “Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth.”) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Levers are used in wheelbarrows, crowbars, scissors and the human arm. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to principle of moments.

items.stem: Design a safe and valid method to investigate how the depth of water affects the pressure at a point. In your answer include the variables, the equipment, the range and number of values of the independent variable, the number of repeats, safety and how the data will be recorded and processed.
items.answer: Make five holes of the same size at 5 cm intervals in a tall plastic bottle, covered with tape; fill with water and keep topped up; remove tape from all holes; measure horizontal distance of each jet at the tray level; repeat three times; plot distance against depth.
items.markingKey: MYP criterion B: 1 independent variable with at least 5 values in a sensible range; 1 dependent variable and how it is measured; 1 at least two controls and how they are controlled; 1 logical step-by-step procedure with equipment; 1 at least 3 repeats and calculation of a mean; 1 relevant safety point (work over a tray or sink and mop spills; cut bottle holes carefully with a hot pin under supervision). Model: Make five holes of the same size at 5 cm intervals in a tall plastic bottle, covered with tape; fill with water and keep topped up; remove tape from all holes; measure horizontal distance of each jet at the tray level; repeat three times; plot distance against depth.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "m/s"?
options: A push or a pull, measured in newtons (N)
The turning effect of a force: moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot
The SI unit of speed (metres per second)
The unit of pressure, equal to 1 N/m²
items.answer: The SI unit of speed (metres per second)
items.markingKey: C. "m/s" is the SI unit of speed (metres per second).

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "terminal velocity"?
options: The constant top speed reached when air resistance equals weight
A push or a pull, measured in newtons (N)
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object
The unit of pressure, equal to 1 N/m²
items.answer: The constant top speed reached when air resistance equals weight
items.markingKey: A. "terminal velocity" is the constant top speed reached when air resistance equals weight.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "force"?
options: The force of gravity on each kilogram; about 10 N/kg on Earth
A push or a pull, measured in newtons (N)
A force that acts at a distance, such as gravity, magnetism or electrostatic force
items.answer: A push or a pull, measured in newtons (N)
items.markingKey: C. "force" is a push or a pull, measured in newtons (N).

items.stem: Explain the difference between the mass of an astronaut and her weight.
items.answer: Mass is the amount of matter, in kg, and is the same everywhere; weight is the force of gravity on that mass, in N, and depends on the gravitational field strength.
items.markingKey: Mass is the amount of matter, in kg, and is the same everywhere; weight is the force of gravity on that mass, in N, and depends on the gravitational field strength. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between anticlockwise moments and clockwise moments.
items.answer: Clockwise moments turn an object one way about the pivot and anticlockwise moments the other way; when they are equal the object balances.
items.markingKey: Clockwise moments turn an object one way about the pivot and anticlockwise moments the other way; when they are equal the object balances. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "A line going down on a distance–time graph means the object is slowing down." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: It means the object is moving back towards the start; slowing down is shown by a curve that becomes less steep.
items.markingKey: It means the object is moving back towards the start; slowing down is shown by a curve that becomes less steep. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "A stationary object has no forces acting on it." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Forces act on it (e.g. weight and reaction force) but they are balanced.
items.markingKey: Forces act on it (e.g. weight and reaction force) but they are balanced. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between non-contact forces and contact forces.
items.answer: Contact forces act when objects touch (friction, tension, air resistance); non-contact forces act at a distance (gravity, magnetism, electrostatic).
items.markingKey: Contact forces act when objects touch (friction, tension, air resistance); non-contact forces act at a distance (gravity, magnetism, electrostatic). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Ingrid writes: "Mass and weight are the same thing." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Mass is in kg and never changes with location; weight is a force in N that changes with gravity.
items.markingKey: Mass is in kg and never changes with location; weight is a force in N that changes with gravity. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A force of 60 N is applied 0.25 m from the pivot of a spanner. Calculate the moment of the force.
items.answer: 15 N m
items.markingKey: M1 moment = F × d = 60 × 0.25; A1 15 N m.

items.stem: A car travels at 72 km/h. Convert this speed to m/s.
items.answer: 20 m/s

items.stem: Ana pulls a box forwards with a force of 120 N. Friction acts backwards with a force of 50 N. Calculate the resultant force and describe the effect on the motion of a box.
items.answer: 70 N forwards; it speeds up
items.markingKey: M1 resultant = 120 − 50; A1 70 N forwards; B1 effect on motion.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Formula 1 aerodynamics shows using forces in design.
items.answer: F1 cars use wings that push the car down onto the track (downforce), increasing friction between tyres and road so the car can corner faster. Engineers balance downforce against air resistance using wind tunnels and computer models.
items.markingKey: Context (F1 cars use wings that push the car down onto the track (downforce), increasing friction between tyres and road so the car can corner faster.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Engineers balance downforce against air resistance using wind tunnels and computer models. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to using forces in design.

items.stem: In an investigation into how the mass of an object affects its weight, state the dependent variable and describe how Amara should measure it.
items.answer: weight read from the newton meter
items.markingKey: 1 mark for naming the dependent variable, 1 mark for a valid measuring method/instrument with unit: weight read from the newton meter.

items.stem: Briefly describe Archimedes and levers and explain what it reveals about principle of moments.
items.answer: Archimedes explained the law of the lever and is quoted as saying “Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth.” Levers are used in wheelbarrows, crowbars, scissors and the human arm.
items.markingKey: Context (Archimedes explained the law of the lever and is quoted as saying “Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth.”) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Levers are used in wheelbarrows, crowbars, scissors and the human arm. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to principle of moments.

items.stem:
Lukas recorded the distance travelled by a cyclist every 10 s using a GPS app (three rides on the same route).

Time / s | Distance / m: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
10 | 63 | 63 | 60
20 | 119 | 122 | 129
30 | 179 | 185 | 182
40 | 246 | 253 | 257
50 | 308 | 308 | 319

Describe the trend shown by the results and explain it using scientific knowledge.
items.answer: The distance increases by about the same amount every 10 s, so the cyclist moves at a roughly constant speed of about 6 m/s. Equal distances in equal times means a constant speed; on a distance–time graph this is a straight line whose gradient gives the speed.
items.markingKey: 1 trend: The distance increases by about the same amount every 10 s, so the cyclist moves at a roughly constant speed of about 6 m/s.; 1 use of data (quote means/values); 1-2 explanation: Equal distances in equal times means a constant speed; on a distance–time graph this is a straight line whose gradient gives the speed.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Seat belts should be compulsory for all passengers in buses."
items.answer: Seat belts make sense on long-distance coaches; for city buses, other safety measures may be more practical.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: passengers keep moving forward when the bus stops suddenly (no force to stop them); reduce injuries in crashes. Arguments against: costly to fit in all buses; standing passengers cannot use them; buses are already relatively safe. Supported judgement: Seat belts make sense on long-distance coaches; for city buses, other safety measures may be more practical.

items.stem: Chloé investigated how the type of surface affects the friction force on a sliding block. The method had this weakness: the block was jerked so the reading kept changing. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: pull with a slow steady motion (or use a motor/pulley) and read while moving steadily
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: pull with a slow steady motion (or use a motor/pulley) and read while moving steadily

items.stem: A 70 kg astronaut travels from Earth (g = 10 N/kg) to the Moon (g = 1.6 N/kg) and Mars (g = 3.7 N/kg). Calculate her weight on each, state her mass on each, and explain the differences.
items.answer: Earth 700 N; Moon 112 N; Mars 259 N; mass 70 kg everywhere. Weight depends on g, which is smaller on the Moon and Mars because they have less mass than Earth; mass is the amount of matter and does not change.
items.markingKey: Earth 700 N; Moon 112 N; Mars 259 N; mass 70 kg everywhere. Weight depends on g, which is smaller on the Moon and Mars because they have less mass than Earth; mass is the amount of matter and does not change.

items.stem: "High-heeled shoes should be banned in buildings with wooden floors." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Requiring heel protectors is a reasonable compromise rather than a ban.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: small heel area creates very high pressure that dents floors; protects historic buildings. Arguments against: personal freedom of choice; heel protectors can increase the area. Supported judgement: Requiring heel protectors is a reasonable compromise rather than a ban. Markbands (15 marks): MYP criterion D (0-8, scaled): 7-8 explains thoroughly how the science is applied to address the issue, discusses and evaluates the implications (moral, ethical, social, economic, political, cultural or environmental), and documents sources consistently; 5-6 explains and discusses; 3-4 outlines; 1-2 states.

items.stem: Define the term "average speed".
items.answer: Total distance travelled ÷ total time taken
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: total distance travelled ÷ total time taken. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "unbalanced forces".
items.answer: Forces that do not cancel, giving a resultant force that changes the motion
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: forces that do not cancel, giving a resultant force that changes the motion. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: In a force diagram, what does the length of an arrow show?
items.answer: The size of the force
items.markingKey: The size of the force. Arrow direction shows force direction.

items.stem: Distinguish between her weight and the mass of an astronaut.
items.answer: Mass is the amount of matter, in kg, and is the same everywhere; weight is the force of gravity on that mass, in N, and depends on the gravitational field strength.
items.markingKey: Mass is the amount of matter, in kg, and is the same everywhere; weight is the force of gravity on that mass, in N, and depends on the gravitational field strength. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between anticlockwise moments and clockwise moments.
items.answer: Clockwise moments turn an object one way about the pivot and anticlockwise moments the other way; when they are equal the object balances.
items.markingKey: Clockwise moments turn an object one way about the pivot and anticlockwise moments the other way; when they are equal the object balances. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Kwame writes: "A line going down on a distance–time graph means the object is slowing down." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It means the object is moving back towards the start; slowing down is shown by a curve that becomes less steep.
items.markingKey: It means the object is moving back towards the start; slowing down is shown by a curve that becomes less steep. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between unbalanced forces and balanced forces.
items.answer: Balanced forces give zero resultant force, so an object stays still or moves at constant velocity; unbalanced forces give a resultant that changes speed or direction.
items.markingKey: Balanced forces give zero resultant force, so an object stays still or moves at constant velocity; unbalanced forces give a resultant that changes speed or direction. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "A moving object must have a force pushing it forward." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: An object can keep moving at constant speed with no resultant force; forces are needed only to change speed or direction.
items.markingKey: An object can keep moving at constant speed with no resultant force; forces are needed only to change speed or direction. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why weight is a force but mass is not.
items.answer: Weight is the pull of gravity on an object, so it has a direction and is measured in newtons; mass is the amount of matter and does not depend on gravity.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Weight is the pull of gravity on an object, so it has a direction and is measured in newtons; mass is the amount of matter and does not depend on gravity. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Leila balanced a metre rule on a pivot at its centre, hung a 2 N weight 20 cm to the left and found the force needed at different distances to the right (three trials each).

Distance on the right / cm | Force needed to balance / N: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
10 | 4.53 | 4.43 | 4.60
20 | 2.23 | 2.22 | 2.19
25 | 1.87 | 1.78 | 1.78
40 | 1.11 | 1.12 | 1.17
50 | 0.88 | 0.92 | 0.91

Calculate the mean force needed to balance when the distance on the right was 20 cm.
items.markingKey: M1 (2.23 + 2.22 + 2.19) ÷ 3; A1 2.21 N (unit and sensible precision).

items.stem: In an investigation into how the height of a ramp affects the average speed of a toy car travelling down it, explain why the same car must be used in every trial.
items.answer: mass and wheels affect speed
items.markingKey: 1 mark: a change in this variable (the same car) would also affect the dependent variable; 1 mark for the specific reason: mass and wheels affect speed. Then only the independent variable is responsible for any change (validity).

items.stem:
Tomás used a data logger to record the speed of a falling cupcake case at different times after release.

Time / s | Speed / m/s: Trial 1 | Trial 2 | Trial 3
0.1 | 0.63 | 0.62 | 0.60
0.2 | 0.90 | 0.90 | 0.90
0.4 | 1.20 | 1.13 | 1.18
0.6 | 1.19 | 1.28 | 1.24
0.8 | 1.27 | 1.28 | 1.25

Calculate the percentage change in the mean speed between 0.1 s and 0.8 s.
items.markingKey: M1 means 0.62 and 1.27; M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100; A1 +105.4% (increase).

items.stem: Ingrid wants to find out how the type of surface affects the friction force on a sliding block. Write a focused research question for this investigation that names both the independent and the dependent variable.
items.answer: How does surface affect force on a newton meter needed to pull the block at a steady speed?
items.markingKey: 1 mark: names the independent variable (surface (wood, carpet, sandpaper, plastic, rubber mat)); 1 mark: names the measurable dependent variable (force on a newton meter needed to pull the block at a steady speed) in a question form.

items.stem: With reference to Apollo 15 hammer and feather (1971), explain how it illustrates gravity and air resistance.
items.answer: Astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon; with no air resistance, they hit the ground together. It confirmed Galileo’s idea that all objects fall with the same acceleration without air resistance.
items.markingKey: Context (Astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon; with no air resistance, they hit the ground together.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: It confirmed Galileo’s idea that all objects fall with the same acceleration without air resistance. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to gravity and air resistance.

items.stem: Kenji writes: "A heavier person always exerts more pressure on the ground." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Pressure depends on area too; a lighter person in stiletto heels can exert more pressure than a heavier person in flat shoes.
items.markingKey: Pressure depends on area too; a lighter person in stiletto heels can exert more pressure than a heavier person in flat shoes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Ana walks 300 m to school at an average speed of 2 m/s. How long does the walk take, in minutes?
items.answer: 2.5 min
items.markingKey: M1 time = distance ÷ speed = 300 ÷ 2 = 150 s; M1 ÷ 60; A1 2.5 min.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Seat belts should be compulsory for all passengers in buses."
items.answer: Seat belts make sense on long-distance coaches; for city buses, other safety measures may be more practical.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: passengers keep moving forward when the bus stops suddenly (no force to stop them); reduce injuries in crashes. Arguments against: costly to fit in all buses; standing passengers cannot use them; buses are already relatively safe. Supported judgement: Seat belts make sense on long-distance coaches; for city buses, other safety measures may be more practical.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Reducing friction is always a good thing."
items.answer: Friction should be reduced where it wastes energy but kept where it is needed for safety and grip.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: saves energy in machines; reduces wear. Arguments against: friction is needed for walking, brakes, gripping and tyres on roads. Supported judgement: Friction should be reduced where it wastes energy but kept where it is needed for safety and grip. items.stem: "Space tourism should be encouraged." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Space tourism brings some benefits, but environmental and fairness concerns mean it should be regulated.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: inspires interest in science; funds development of new technology. Arguments against: huge fuel use and emissions per passenger; only for the very wealthy; safety risks. Supported judgement: Space tourism brings some benefits, but environmental and fairness concerns mean it should be regulated. items.stem: Diego investigated how the depth of water affects the pressure at a point. The method had this weakness: the water level dropped during the measurements. Evaluate how this weakness affects the validity of the results and suggest an improvement to the method.
items.answer: keep a hose running in so the level stays at the top mark
items.markingKey: 1 identifies how the weakness introduces error or an uncontrolled variable; 1 states the effect on the results/conclusion; 1-2 a specific, practical improvement: keep a hose running in so the level stays at the top mark
